subject: Hydraulics

questions.question: Prove that the velocity distribution for steady laminar flow in a circular pipe is parabolic (Hagen-Poiseuille law) and show that the maximum velocity is twice the average flow velocity.
Explain Prandtl's mixing length theory. Show that the velocity distribution in pipes for turbulent flow is logarithmic. Derive an expression for head loss due to sudden expansion in a pipeline.
What are hydrodynamically smooth and rough boundaries? State the boundary roughness criteria based on roughness Reynolds number and explain Nikuradse's sand roughness experiment.

What are HGL (Hydraulic Gradient Line) and TEL (Total Energy Line)? Draw HGL and TEL showing elevation, pressure, and velocity heads for uniform and non-uniform pipes with real fluid flow, including pump and turbine installations.

Explain the three-reservoir problem in branching pipes. State the governing continuity and energy equations, and describe the step-by-step iterative procedure to determine the direction of flow and discharge in each branch pipe.
Explain the Hardy Cross method of pipe network analysis for balancing heads and balancing flows. Derive the expression for flow correction ΔQ in a closed pipe loop.

A pipeline of 600 mm diameter is 1.5 km long. To increase the discharge, another pipe of the same diameter is introduced parallel to the first in the second half of its length. If f = 0.01 and head at inlet is 300 mm, calculate the percentage increase in discharge.

Describe with sketches the variation of water hammer pressure with time (at the valve end and at the midpoint of the pipe) in a long pipeline leading from a reservoir when the downstream valve is suddenly closed.

Derive the Allievi equation for water hammer pressure rise due to gradual closure of a valve in a pipeline. What is the role of surge tanks in hydropower systems, and classify different types of surge tanks.

Derive the conditions for the hydraulically most efficient trapezoidal and rectangular channel sections. Show that for the most efficient trapezoidal section, hydraulic radius R = y/2 and the side slope angle is 60° to the horizontal.
Find an expression for the theoretical depth for maximum velocity and maximum discharge in a closed circular channel in terms of diameter d.
Draw and explain Shields diagram. Describe how an unlined alluvial channel is designed based on the tractive force method (critical shear stress approach).

Define Specific Energy and draw the specific energy curve for a rectangular channel. Derive expressions for critical depth yc, critical velocity Vc, and minimum specific energy Emin in terms of discharge per unit width q.

questions.text: Derive the Darcy-Weisbach Equation for head loss due to friction in commercial pipes: $h_f = \frac{f L v^2}{2 g D}$. Discuss the Moody Diagram and explain the variations of friction factor $f$ in laminar ($f = 64/Re$), transitional, smooth turbulent, and fully rough turbulent flow regimes.
questions.solutionOutline: Equating shear resisting force tau_0 * pi D L to pressure force Delta p * pi D^2 / 4 yields h_f = 4 tau_0 L / (rho g D). Defining friction factor f = 8 tau_0 / (rho v^2) gives Darcy-Weisbach equation h_f = f L v^2 / (2g D). Moody diagram plots f vs Re for varying relative roughness k_s/D. Laminar (Re < 2000): f = 64/Re (independent of roughness). Smooth turbulent: laminar sublayer submerges surface asperities; f depends only on Re. Fully rough: asperities penetrate sublayer; f depends solely on k_s/D (von Karman equation 1/sqrt(f) = 2 log10(D/k_s) + 1.14).

questions.text: Analyze Complex Pipe Networks using the Hardy Cross Method. Detail the method of balancing heads around closed loops ($\Delta Q = -\frac{\sum r Q_0 |Q_0|^{n-1}}{\sum n r |Q_0|^{n-1}}$) and solve for corrected flow rates in a distribution network.
questions.solutionOutline: Iterative loop method based on two physical laws: 1) Continuity at every junction sum Q_in = sum Q_out; 2) Zero algebraic sum of head losses around every closed loop sum h_f = sum r Q^n = 0 (Darcy n=2 or Hazen-Williams n=1.852). Assume initial flow Q0 satisfying continuity. Flow correction Delta Q = -sum(r Q0 |Q0|) / sum(2 r |Q0|). Correct flows Q = Q0 + Delta Q (subtracting for pipes shared between adjacent loops), repeating until Delta Q is negligible.

questions.text: Explain Water Hammer in pipelines. Derive the Joukowsky formula for acoustic pressure surge $\Delta p = \rho c v_0$ for instantaneous valve closure. Differentiate between rapid and slow valve closure using critical closure time $t_c = \frac{2L}{c}$, and explain the function of surge tanks.
questions.solutionOutline: Pressure wave generated by sudden destruction of kinetic energy upon rapid valve closure. Applying impulse-momentum equation to acoustic wavefront traveling at wave speed c = sqrt((K/rho) / [1 + (K D / E t)]): Delta p * A * dt = rho (A c dt) v_0 => Delta p = rho c v_0. Acoustic head surge Delta H = c v_0 / g. Critical time t_c = 2L/c (round-trip travel time of pressure wave). Rapid closure (t_v <= t_c): full Joukowsky surge occurs. Slow closure (t_v > t_c): relief wave attenuates surge Delta p_max = 2 rho L v_0 / t_v. Surge tank absorbs rejected water volume, dampening pressure oscillations.

questions.text: Derive Chezy's and Manning's equations for uniform flow in open channels: $v = \frac{1}{n} R^{2/3} S_0^{1/2}$. Derive the geometric conditions for the Most Economically Efficient Hydraulic Section for: (a) Rectangular channel ($b = 2y$), and (b) Trapezoidal channel ($R = y/2$, side slope $60^\circ$).
questions.solutionOutline: Most efficient section delivers maximum discharge for given cross-sectional area A, which requires minimizing wetted perimeter P (maximizing hydraulic radius R = A/P). Rectangular channel: A = b y, P = b + 2y = A/y + 2y. dP/dy = -A/y^2 + 2 = 0 => b = 2y and R = y/2. Trapezoidal channel: A = (b + m y) y, P = b + 2y sqrt(1 + m^2). Minimizing P with respect to y and side slope m yields: hydraulic radius R = y/2; top width T = 2 * (sloping side length); optimum side slope m = 1/sqrt(3) (theta = 60 deg, half of regular hexagon).

questions.chapter: Energy and Momentum Principles in Open Channel Flow
questions.text: Explain Specific Energy $E = y + \frac{v^2}{2g} = y + \frac{Q^2}{2g A^2}$ in open channels. Derive Critical Depth $y_c = \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}$, minimum specific energy $E_{min} = 1.5 y_c$, and Critical Velocity ($Fr = 1$) for a rectangular channel.
questions.solutionOutline: Specific energy is energy per unit weight of fluid measured relative to channel bottom. For rectangular channel of width b with discharge per unit width q = Q/b: E = y + q^2 / (2g y^2). Critical depth corresponds to minimum specific energy: dE/dy = 1 - q^2 / (g y^3) = 0 => y_c = (q^2 / g)^(1/3). Substituting y_c: E_min = y_c + y_c / 2 = 1.5 y_c. Critical velocity v_c = sqrt(g y_c) => Froude number Fr = v_c / sqrt(g y_c) = 1. Subcritical flow (Fr < 1, y > y_c); Supercritical flow (Fr > 1, y < y_c).

questions.chapter: Energy and Momentum Principles in Open Channel Flow
questions.text: Explain Specific Force (Momentum Function) $M = \frac{Q^2}{g A} + \bar{z} A$ in open channel hydraulics. Prove that critical flow occurs at minimum specific force and contrast the specific force curve with the specific energy curve.
questions.solutionOutline: Specific force is sum of momentum flux per unit weight and hydrostatic pressure force: M = Q^2 / (g A) + z_bar A. In hydraulic jumps and sudden transitions where external friction is negligible, momentum is conserved: M1 = M2. Differentiating with respect to depth y: dM/dy = -Q^2 / (g A^2) dA/dy + d(z_bar A)/dy. Since dA/dy = T (top width) and d(z_bar A)/dy = A: dM/dy = A (1 - Q^2 T / (g A^3)) = A (1 - Fr^2). Setting dM/dy = 0 yields Fr = 1, proving minimum specific force occurs at critical depth.

questions.chapter: Rapidly Varied Flow in Open Channels
questions.text: Derive the Hydraulic Jump Conjugate Depth (Bélanger's) Equation: $\frac{y_2}{y_1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8 Fr_1^2} - 1\right)$. Derive energy loss in a jump $\Delta E = \frac{(y_2 - y_1)^3}{4 y_1 y_2}$ and explain USBR Stilling Basins for hydraulic energy dissipation.
questions.solutionOutline: Occurs when supercritical stream abruptly jumps to subcritical state with turbulent energy dissipation. Equating specific force M1 = M2 for rectangular channel: q^2/(g y1) + y1^2/2 = q^2/(g y2) + y2^2/2. Rearranging gives y2/y1 = 0.5 * (sqrt(1 + 8 Fr1^2) - 1). Energy loss Delta E = E1 - E2 = (y1 + v1^2/2g) - (y2 + v2^2/2g) = (y2 - y1)^3 / (4 y1 y2). USBR Stilling basins (Type II, III, IV) use chute blocks, baffle piers, and end sills to shorten jump length and stabilize jump within paved concrete apron.

questions.chapter: Rapidly Varied Flow in Open Channels
questions.text: Classify Hydraulic Jumps based on upstream Froude Number ($Fr_1$): Undular ($1 < Fr_1 < 1.7$), Weak ($1.7 < Fr_1 < 2.5$), Oscillating ($2.5 < Fr_1 < 4.5$), Steady ($4.5 < Fr_1 < 9$), and Strong ($Fr_1 > 9$).
questions.solutionOutline: Classification (USBR): Fr1=1 to 1.7 (Undular: standing surface waves, negligible energy dissipation <5%); Fr1=1.7 to 2.5 (Weak: small rollers form, smooth water surface, energy loss 5-18%); Fr1=2.5 to 4.5 (Oscillating: pulsating jet moving from floor to surface, generates destructive waves downstream, avoid in stilling basins); Fr1=4.5 to 9.0 (Steady jump: stable, well-balanced roller, 45-70% energy dissipation, ideal for stilling basins); Fr1 > 9.0 (Strong/Chappy jump: violent intermittent slug flow, >70% energy dissipation).

questions.chapter: Gradually Varied Flow in Open Channels
questions.text: Derive the Dynamic Equation of Gradually Varied Flow (GVF): $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{S_0 - S_f}{1 - Fr^2}$. Classify GVF surface profiles on Mild ($M_1, M_2, M_3$), Steep ($S_1, S_2, S_3$), Critical ($C_1, C_3$), Horizontal ($H_2, H_3$), and Adverse ($A_2, A_3$) channel slopes.
questions.solutionOutline: Total energy H = z + y + v^2/2g. Differentiating with respect to x: dH/dx = dz/dx + dy/dx + d(v^2/2g)/dx. Since dH/dx = -S_f, dz/dx = -S_0, and d(v^2/2g)/dx = -Fr^2 dy/dx: -S_f = -S_0 + dy/dx (1 - Fr^2) => dy/dx = (S_0 - S_f) / (1 - Fr^2). Mild slope (y_n > y_c): M1 (y > y_n > y_c, backwater curve behind dam), M2 (y_n > y > y_c, drawdown into drop), M3 (y_n > y_c > y, supercritical flow). Steep slope (y_c > y_n): S1, S2, S3 profiles.

questions.chapter: Gradually Varied Flow in Open Channels
questions.text: Explain numerical computation of GVF water surface profiles: Direct Step Method and Standard Step Method. State their governing equations, step sequence, and control section boundary conditions.
questions.solutionOutline: Direct step method (prismatic channels): chooses depth increment Delta y and solves for distance step Delta x = (E2 - E1) / (S_0 - S_f_avg), marching step-by-step from control section. Standard step method (natural non-prismatic rivers): divides channel into fixed distance reaches Delta x and iteratively solves for unknown depth y2 using trial-and-error until total energy equation H2 = H1 + h_f + h_e balances within tolerance. Subcritical control is downstream (computation marches upstream); supercritical control is upstream.

questions.chapter: Energy and Momentum Principles in Open Channel Flow
questions.text: Explain Channel Transitions: flow over a smooth upward hump ($\Delta z$) and channel width constriction ($\Delta b$). Determine the critical hump height $\Delta z_c$ and critical width $b_{min}$ to avoid upstream backwater choking.
questions.solutionOutline: Bernoulli between section 1 and constricted section 2: E1 = E2 + Delta z. For subcritical approach flow, water surface dips over hump. Critical hump height occurs when flow at section 2 reaches critical state (E2 = E_min = 1.5 y_c): Delta z_c = E1 - E_min. If Delta z > Delta z_c, channel chokes, raising upstream depth y1. Similarly, width constriction increases discharge per unit width q2 = Q/b2; minimum width to avoid choking b_min = Q / sqrt(g y_c^3) = Q / sqrt(g (2/3 E1)^3).

questions.text: Explain Spatially Varied Flow (SVF) with increasing and decreasing discharge. Derive the dynamic equation for side weir channels and lateral spillway troughs.
questions.solutionOutline: Discharge varies along channel length (dQ/dx != 0). Increasing discharge (lateral inflow into spillway channel): incoming water carries no x-momentum; mixing causes turbulent kinetic energy loss, requiring momentum equation for formulation: dy/dx = [S_0 - S_f - 2 Q q / (g A^2)] / [1 - Fr^2]. Decreasing discharge (side weir diversion): diverted water leaves with channel velocity without impacting momentum of remaining stream, allowing energy equation to be applied directly.

questions.text: Explain Surges (Positive and Negative Surges) in open channels following rapid gate closure or opening. Derive the celerity formula for a solitary gravity wave $c = \sqrt{g y}$ and continuity/momentum relations across the surge front.
questions.solutionOutline: Unsteady open-channel wave front created by sudden operation of sluice gates. Positive surge increases water depth (steepens as it propagates due to higher wave speed in deeper water, forming traveling hydraulic bore). Negative surge decreases water depth (flattens out with distance). Applying continuity and momentum across surge traveling at absolute velocity V_w: relative velocity v_r1 = v1 - V_w, v_r2 = v2 - V_w. Wave celerity for small disturbance c = sqrt(g y).
